lines.text: Five thousand years along one river: pharaohs and pyramids, Greeks and Romans, caliphs and sultans, and a modern nation. This is the story of Egypt.
It all begins with the Nile. Its yearly floods laid a ribbon of rich farmland through the desert, and on that ribbon a civilisation grew.
Along the lower Nile, kings called pharaohs would rule for some three thousand years, leaving temples, hieroglyphs and a faith devoted to the afterlife.
At Saqqara, around 2640 BCE, the official Imhotep stacked stone platforms into a Step Pyramid for King Djoser, the first great stone building on Earth.
Less than a century later rose the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza, for thousands of years the tallest building in the world, and still standing.
Beside it, carved from the bedrock, the Great Sphinx, a lion with a human face, most likely made for the pharaoh Khafre.
At Thebes, pharaoh after pharaoh added to the temples of Karnak, a forest of giant columns raised to the god Amun over two thousand years.
By the New Kingdom, kings were no longer buried under pyramids but in painted tombs cut into the rock of the Valley of the Kings.
One of them was Tutankhamun, a boy king who died in his teens. His tomb, found almost untouched in 1922, made him the most famous pharaoh of all.
Then came Ramesses the Second, who ruled for over sixty years, fought the Hittites at Kadesh and later signed one of the earliest peace treaties we know.
In the far south he carved Abu Simbel into a cliff, fronted by four colossal statues of himself. In the 1960s it was moved, block by block, above the rising Nile.
Centuries later, in 331 BCE, Alexander the Great founded a new city on the coast, Alexandria, which would become one of the most learned cities of the ancient world.
After Alexander, his general Ptolemy and his heirs ruled Egypt as Greek kings, with their great Library at Alexandria.
On the island of Pharos they raised a towering lighthouse to guide ships into the harbour, one of the wonders of the ancient world.
In 196 BCE a royal decree was carved in three scripts on one stone. Found at Rosetta, it later gave Champollion the key to reading hieroglyphs.
The last of the Ptolemies was Cleopatra, who allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony to keep Egypt free. After her death, it became a Roman province.
Long after the Arab conquest, a Shia dynasty from North Africa, the Fatimids, took Egypt in the tenth century and made it the heart of their caliphate.
Beside the Nile they founded a new capital, Cairo, which would grow into one of the greatest cities of Africa and the Islamic world.
A year later they founded the mosque of al-Azhar, which became a centre of learning and one of the oldest universities still at work.
In the twelfth century Saladin, a Kurdish general, ruled Egypt and Syria, united Muslim lands against the Crusaders and took back Jerusalem.
Then the Mamluks, once slave soldiers, seized power. They stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut, drove out the last Crusaders and filled Cairo with monuments.
Under the Ottomans, a governor named Muhammad Ali took charge in the early 1800s and built Egypt into a strong state of its own.
In 1869 the Suez Canal opened, joining the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and cutting thousands of kilometres off the voyage between Europe and Asia.
In 1898 Umm Kulthum was born, the singer whose voice would hold the whole Arab world spellbound.
Naguib Mahfouz, born in 1911, would write the life of Cairo in his novels and become the first Arabic writer to win the Nobel Prize.
Gamal Abdel Nasser, born in 1918, would help overthrow the king, take over the Suez Canal and become the voice of Arab unity.
In the same year came Anwar Sadat, who would follow Nasser, go to war with Israel in 1973 and then make peace with it.
In 1922 Britain, which had occupied Egypt since 1882, recognised its independence as a kingdom.
Twenty years later, the Second World War reached Egypt. At El Alamein, Montgomery's army broke the German and Italian advance on the Suez Canal.
In 1952 a group of army officers overthrew the monarchy, and Egypt soon became a republic.
Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, born in 1954, would rise through the army, take power in 2013 and become president the following year.
In 1956 Nasser took over the Suez Canal. Britain, France and Israel attacked, but were forced to withdraw, and Egypt kept its canal.
In 1970 the Aswan High Dam was finished with Soviet help. It tamed the Nile's floods and lit the country, but drowned Nubian lands.
In 1992 Mohamed Salah was born, the footballer who would become a star at Liverpool and a hero across Egypt.
In 2002 Alexandria opened a great new library, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, in memory of the ancient one.
In 2011 crowds filled Tahrir Square in Cairo, and after thirty years in power, Hosni Mubarak was forced out.
And in 2025 the Grand Egyptian Museum opened fully beside the pyramids of Giza, bringing the treasures of the pharaohs home.
The pharaohs are long gone, but the Nile still flows, and Egypt still lives along it.
